title: Insolation-forced oceanic changes triggered the Eurasian Ice Sheet collapse and the Last Termination
abstract: Abstract The collapse of Northern Hemisphere ice sheets has been deemed as a trigger for the chain of positive climate feedback during glacial terminations in Quaternary. Increasing boreal summer insolation is considered the ultimate driver of their collapse, however, the initiating mechanisms remain elusive. Here we report an unambiguous warming trend in the southern Nordic Seas, which coincides with the initial phase of Northern Hemisphere summer insolation increase at the end of the Last Glacial Maximum. A subsequent phase of surface cooling is observed, closely corresponding to the massive freshwater discharge attributed to the meltwater pulse at 19ka BP. Our reconstructions demonstrate that the initial collapse of Northern Hemisphere ice sheets during the Last Termination occurred in Eurasian Ice Sheet, driven by a chain of oceanic responses to the insolation increase. Specifically, increasing boreal insolation induced a northward migration of the mid-latitude Westerlies under a positive NAO phase, promoting poleward oceanic heat transport and hence subsequent warming in Nordic Seas, thereby accelerating the ablation of the marine-based Eurasian Ice Shelves. This led to a catastrophic release of icebergs into Nordic Seas, eventually triggering a series of ocean circulation feedbacks that further promoted the deglaciation.

title: On the Fidelity of Oxygen Isotope‐Based Sea Level Reconstructions: A Case Study of Marine Isotope Stage 3
abstract: Abstract Although foraminiferal oxygen isotope records (δ 18 O F ) have long been used to develop time‐continuous estimates of past global ice volume, growing evidence indicates that the ice volume and temperature contributions to δ 18 O F diverge considerably over the last glacial cycle. Across Marine Isotope Stage 3 (MIS 3; 57 to 29 ka), estimates of peak global sea level based on δ 18 O F are ∼30 m lower than reconstructions based on recent glacial geology, geologic sea‐level records, and glacial isostatic adjustment (GIA) modeling approaches. Here we address this mismatch by quantifying uncertainties in converting δ 18 O F to global sea level during MIS 3. We review the geochemical tools to assess the contributions of ocean temperature, diagenesis, and the isotopic composition of ice sheets to δ 18 O F records across MIS 3. We show that recent advances in our understanding of these and other factors that contribute uncertainty (e.g., global sea level during the Last Glacial Maximum) help to explain the MIS 3 gap between global sea level estimates based on δ 18 O F and GIA analyses of geologic sea‐level records. We find that the accuracy and precision of MIS 3 ocean temperature reconstructions is likely a key contributor, and various MIS 3 temperature reconstructions can reduce the “gap” by 30%–70% (∼10–20 m). Future improvements in the precision of temperature reconstructions will better constrain the ice volume component of δ 18 O F records. Ultimately, assessing the fidelity of δ 18 O F as a proxy for global ice volume is key to disentangling the feedbacks between climate and ice sheets over the Pleistocene.

title: Antarctic sea ice response to meltwater due to Antarctic ice sheet mass loss in a multi-model ensemble
abstract: Climate models typically do not include meltwater entering the Southern Ocean due to Antarctic ice sheet mass loss. Previous work shows this meltwater drives sea ice growth, but the varying responses have been difficult to compare across models. We ran 11 climate models using the same meltwater input and found a wide range of sea ice responses depending on the background state in each model. Understanding this uncertainty in response is important for future projections of Antarctic sea ice.

title: Transition of Glacial Regimes Recorded at IODP Site U1524 in the Ross Sea, Antarctica, Over the Last 800 Thousand Years
abstract: Abstract Reconstructing past interactions between the West Antarctic Ice Sheet (WAIS) and changing environmental conditions in the Ross Sea region can help determine long‐term WAIS stability. Existing sedimentary records reveal changes to oceanography, sea ice and ice sheet extent over the glacial‐interglacial cycles of the last ∼800 kyr. There are, however, few high‐resolution, ice‐proximal records extending to before the Last Glacial Maximum. Here, we examine a broad suite of lithological, biogenic, physical property and geochemical data from International Ocean Discovery Program (IODP) Site U1524 from the continental rise in the central Ross Sea. An age model spanning the last ∼800 kyr is established within constraints provided by biostratigraphy, palaeomagnetism and foraminifera amino acid racemization. Lithofacies analysis reveals the pattern of glacial advance and interglacial retreat. Enhanced delivery of ice rafted debris and preservation of radiolaria occurs during deglacial and interglacial periods, with fine‐grained diatom‐bearing to diatom‐rich sediments deposited during glacial periods. Foraminifera are preserved during the latest parts of the Marine Isotope Stage (MIS) 11 and 9 interglacials. Proxy data apparently suggest higher productivity during glacial periods, which is explained by reworking and redeposition of older detritus from the continental shelf. A change in the character of glacial period sediments after MIS 7 (∼200 kyr ago) suggests there was a less extensive grounded ice sheet during the last two glacial periods. Together, these results provide a detailed reconstruction of mid‐ to late‐Pleistocene ocean–ice sheet interactions, improving understanding of how the Ross Sea region may respond to ongoing climate change.

title: Sea-level contribution from Thwaites Glacier doubles in an observation-constrained ice-sheet model
abstract: Abstract Thwaites Glacier is a major contributor to Antarctic mass loss and a key source of uncertainty in future sea-level rise. Ocean-driven melting at its grounding line drives rapid retreat, yet most models treat the transition between grounded and floating ice as a sharp boundary, neglecting kilometer-scale seawater intrusions that develop as the grounding line migrates and forms a grounding zone. Here, we show that actively-melting grounding zones are required to reproduce nearly three decades of observed retreat, thinning, and acceleration of Thwaites Glacier in a calibrated ice-sheet model, with successful reconstruction occurring only when grounding zones are represented as 2-5 km wide regions. Extending this model forward, we show that grounding-zone processes govern glacier’s detachment from stabilizing seafloor ridges, enabling unpinning as early as 2038 and producing up to 30 ± 6 mm of global mean sea-level rise by 2100 - approximately double previous projections even without additional climate warming.

title: Hydroclimate of northeast Mexico since the Last Glacial Maximum and possible influence of the Caribbean Low-Level Jet
abstract: The rise in average temperature of Mexico has been consistent with persistent droughts over the last decades and socio-economic disruptions in key agricultural regions. This study provided new hydroclimate data up to the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) with a paleoclimate record from the Cieneguilla Basin of northeast Mexico. A multi-proxy approach reconstructed the millennial-to-orbital scale near-surface processes, including the hydrological balance-driven watershed erosion and evaporation-induced salinity at western limit of the Sierra Madre Oriental Mountains, and revealed a distinct transition from an overall wetter deglaciation to drier Holocene. Its resemblance with reconstructed dynamics of the Great Plains low-level jet (GPLLJ) in south-central US supported possible role of the Caribbean Low-Level Jet (CLLJ) in moisture transport. Wetter conditions over the deglaciation aligned with a phase of more spring insolation, less autumn insolation, cooler SSTs in Gulf of Mexico and tropical Atlantic, and strong GPLLJ. The early-to-middle Holocene aridification, in phase with less spring insolation and weak GPLLJ, was marked by reduced erosion, enhanced carbonate deposition and higher contribution from isotopically enriched organic matter likely from the drought tolerant C 4 /CAM plants. The early Holocene aridification across northeast Mexico and contemporary warming in tropical Atlantic might be revealing the diminished influence of meridional CLLJ flow, possibly from a shifting North Atlantic Subtropical High.

title: legoESM: a modular, differentiable, multiscale, AI-ready Earth system model built with AI agents
abstract: arXiv:2610.11883v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Earth system models (ESMs) have grown tremendously in realism, yet key uncertainties persist in the climate response to greenhouse-gas forcing, particularly due to cloud radiative feedbacks. In addition, their software architecture was not designed for accelerator hardware or modern artificial intelligence (AI). Here we present legoESM, a composable, differentiable, multiscale ESM written in JAX. It builds on decades of community-developed parameterizations and numerical methods, recast in a unified framework by AI coding agents under a human-specified scientific contract and verified through benchmarking. Dynamical cores, physics schemes, grids, complexity levels and components are swappable like building blocks, and can use conventional physics or machine-learned emulators. A single code base spans metre-scale large-eddy simulation to global simulations and weather to climate. End-to-end differentiability enables gradient-based calibration, variational data assimilation and online training. legoESM modular architecture enables systematic evaluation of diverse model variants to explore structural uncertainty and test hypotheses. legoESM produces realistic simulations across scales, reduces land-surface temperature bias through gradient-based calibration, and scales efficiently on GPUs to kilometer-scale simulations. It offers an open, community infrastructure for hypothesis testing, research and teaching in Earth sciences and a template for multiscale physical systems.

title: Subglacial Radar Reflectivity Estimation Considering Volumetric Scattering Loss from Englacial Dielectric Inhomogeneities
abstract: To improve the accuracy of subglacial reflectivity estimation using ice-sounding radar, this study proposes a method that explicitly incorporates volumetric scattering loss caused by englacial dielectric inhomogeneities. Particle scattering from englacial dielectric inhomogeneities is accounted for using Rayleigh and Mie theory, with the applicable formulation selected according to the relationship between the characteristic size of the inhomogeneities and the radar wavelength. The resulting scattering loss is incorporated into the conventional propagation-loss model to obtain corrected basal reflectivity estimates. Main simulations of bedrock–subglacial water and bedrock–sediment transitions were conducted at a center frequency of 200 MHz using an effective scatterer radius of 0.2 mm and porosities of 0.5% and 0.8%. Supplementary simulations were further performed at 60 MHz, corresponding to the operating frequency of the airborne radar system used in the field experiments. Compared with the conventional attenuation-correction method, the proposed method produced reflectivity estimates closer to the prescribed reference values and reduced the RMSE by approximately 29.2–34.8%. The method was further validated using airborne radar data from Lake Snow Eagle, Lake Vostok, the Lambert Glacier Basin, and Dome A. At Lake Vostok, the absolute deviation from the reference value was reduced from 0.85 to 0.47 dB, while at Dome A it was reduced from 1.01 to 0.71 dB. These results demonstrate that explicitly accounting for volumetric scattering loss can reduce systematic reflectivity bias and improve the accuracy and reliability of subglacial water, sediment, and bedrock characterization.

title: Cryosphere hazards under weather and climate extremes in the Hindu Kush Himalaya: The cryosphere hazard interaction pathways (CHiP) framework
abstract: The Hindu Kush Himalaya has emerged as a hotspot of cryosphere hazards due to climate change. While long-term warming governs glacier, snow, and permafrost evolution, weather and climate extremes (WCEs) often control hazard timing and magnitude. However, understanding of WCEs–cryosphere interactions remain limited and existing preconditioning-triggering concepts have examined WCEs impact on cryosphere components in isolation rather than applying a single framework. Here, we synthesize recent evidence and propose the Cryosphere Hazard Interaction Pathways (CHiP) Framework under WCEs. The framework links WCEs to cryosphere hazards via direct triggering (P1), indirect or lagged response (P2). These pathways drive compound and cascading hazards across the region. Integrating CHiP under WCEs into monitoring, hazard investigation, and early warning is essential for improving multi-hazard risk assessment and climate-resilient adaptation in high-mountain regions.

title: Assessment of an updated polar stratospheric cloud parameterisation for the UK Earth System Model (UKESM1.1) within the UK Met Office Unified Model (v13.9) using  CALIOP and MLS observations
abstract: The UK Earth System Model is updated with an improved polar stratospheric cloud scheme. The performance of the scheme is evaluated against satellite data. While the model fails to form the full range of observed ice, the scheme improves its ability to represent different polar stratospheric cloud types and their variations. This brings the model closer to satellite observations and highlights the need for further development to capture the polar stratospheric clouds with high number densities.

title: A long-term trend toward wetter conditions during MIS 2 inferred from modern-monitoring-based stalagmite multi-proxy records from Remi Cave, Central China
abstract: The ongoing debate regarding the spatial pattern of precipitation and effective moisture changes in monsoonal eastern China during the Marine Isotope Stage 2 (MIS 2) centers on the hydroclimatic evolution of the middle and lower Yangtze River Valley. Here, we present an approximately four-year (December 2020 to December 2024) systematic modern monitoring program and multi-proxy records (δ 18 O, δ 13 C, Mg/Ca, Sr/Ca, Ba/Ca) from stalagmite RM4 in Remi cave, Hunan Province, Central China, spanning ∼25.7‒14.5 kyr BP. Based on modern monitoring results and cross-validation among multi-proxy records, the δ 13 C values and Sr/Ca and Ba/Ca ratios in the stalagmite RM4 record are interpreted as qualitative indicators of an integrated effective-moisture signal, whereas variations in RM4 δ 18 O appear to be mainly associated with large-scale atmospheric circulation. During the ∼25.7–14.5 kyr BP interval, the δ 13 C, Sr/Ca, and Ba/Ca records from stalagmite RM4, complemented by various records from nearby stalagmites and peat bogs, indicate an overall long-term trend toward increased effective moisture in central China. This trend is consistent with precipitation reconstructions from northeastern China, but contrasts with contemporaneous long-term drying trends reported in northern and southern China, which may point to a quadrupole-like pattern of hydroclimatic change across monsoonal eastern China. We suggest that this marked spatial heterogeneity in hydroclimate may have been modulated by zonal sea surface temperature gradients across the tropical Pacific, which may have influenced the position and intensity of the West Pacific subtropical high and possibly triggered a cyclonic anomaly to its north through the western North Pacific anomalous anticyclone. Our results highlight the value of integrating modern cave monitoring, with multi-proxy records from various archives for understanding the controlling mechanisms of stalagmite proxy records.

title: Biological pump variations in the northeastern Indian Ocean since the last glaciation: evidence from coccolithophores
abstract: The biological pump (BP) constitutes a key component of the global carbon cycle by mediating the export of organic carbon from the surface ocean to the deep sea. However, long-term variability of BP strength in the northeastern Indian Ocean (NEIO), particularly within the strongly stratified Bay of Bengal (BoB), remains inadequately constrained due to the complex interplay between monsoon forcing and freshwater-induced stratification. Here, we present a high-resolution reconstruction of BP variability over the last ∼ 53 kyr based on primary productivity (PP) estimates derived from quantitative analyses of coccolithophore assemblages in a sediment core from the southern BoB. Coccoliths are abundant and well preserved throughout the record, with assemblages dominated by Florisphaera profunda , Gephyrocapsa oceanica , and Emiliania huxleyi . The reconstructed PP record exhibits pronounced glacial–interglacial (G–IG) variability, characterized by reduced productivity during the Last Glacial Maximum, followed by a progressive increase during the deglaciation and a peak in the Early Holocene. Principal component analysis of productivity records across the Indian Ocean (IO) identifies G–IG climate variability as the dominant mode of basin-scale productivity change while distinguishing secondary atmospheric and hydrological controls on regional productivity. Comparison with PP records from other sectors of the IO further highlights marked spatial heterogeneity in BP responses to basin-scale climatic forcing. In the NEIO, productivity was primarily controlled by G–IG changes in upper-ocean stratification and nutrient availability driven by sea level fluctuations and freshwater forcing, whereas secondary variability reflects the distinct atmospheric and hydrological expressions of the Indian Summer Monsoon. Our findings indicate that regional hydrographic processes governed the expression of basin-scale climatic forcing, distinguishing the freshwater-controlled NEIO from the wind-driven upwelling systems of the western tropical IO.

title: Biomarkers and diatoms as tracers of phytoplankton communities and past sea ice conditions in the southwestern Ross Sea, Antarctica: drivers and variability over the last 200 years
abstract: Abstract. The Ross Sea, Antarctica, is among the most seasonally productive areas globally, where different classes of phytoplankton, such as diatoms and haptophytes (Phaeocystis antarctica), play key roles in marine ecosystems and the carbon cycle. Sea ice dynamics strongly influence Ross Sea phytoplankton blooms, yet the effects of recent sea ice changes on bloom composition and productivity remain poorly constrained. Seasonally resolved observational records of past Ross Sea phytoplankton and sea ice variability are too short to understand potential future changes in sea ice extent, phytoplankton productivity and community composition, and the resulting consequences on climate. In this study, we investigated phytoplankton-derived lipid biomarkers (fatty acids, highly branched isoprenoids; HBIs, sterols) and diatom assemblages in six marine sediment core tops and three short sediment cores collected along a north-south transect spanning two seasonally recurring polynyas in McMurdo Sound and Terra Nova Bay, to assess how sea ice dynamics and phytoplankton communities drive biomarker signatures and diatom assemblages archived in sediments. For the core-tops, we find that the proportion of open-ocean diatom species and bacterial fatty acid concentrations in core top samples increases towards the southern end of the transect near McMurdo Sound, which is driven by lower summer sea ice extent, a phytoplankton community dominated by diatoms, and higher summer biomass in McMurdo Sound. In contrast, diatom assemblages shift towards sea ice-associated diatoms in the northern end of the transect, characterised by increased concentrations of sea ice diatom-derived fatty acids, sterols, and HBIs (PIPSO25), driven by greater sea ice concentrations. Similarly, Phaeocystis antarctica-derived fatty acid biomarkers increased towards the northern end of the transect, likely driven by differences in the phytoplankton community. For the short cores, we show that an exponential decrease in the fatty acid biomarker signal in the top ~20 cm of sediment is driven by processes such as bacterial biogenesis. Although phytoplankton-derived fatty acids show little change in community composition over the last 200 years, Fragilariopsis curta and PIPSO25 indicate increasing sea ice extent, accompanied by declining Chaetoceros resting spores and open ocean diatom species in the southwestern Ross Sea. Overall, our records reveal a 200-year increasing sea ice trend, consistent with existing regional sea ice extent reconstructions from ice cores. Overall, biomarkers in the southwestern Ross Sea sediment independently distinguish between pelagic diatoms, P. antarctica, and sea ice-associated diatoms, offering a valuable tool for developing decadal resolution records of sea ice and phytoplankton community changes.

title: Interannual and seasonal evolution of supraglacial drainage systems on Nivlisen Ice Shelf, East Antarctica
abstract: Supraglacial drainage systems mediate meltwater transport over ice shelves and may influence their stability. Our mapping of Nivlisen Ice Shelf from satellite imagery shows significant variation in interannual and seasonal drainage extent. During warm summers, channels become increasingly connected, redistributing meltwater from high to low elevations across the ice shelf. Channel location is controlled by ice shelf structure, and annual extent is correlated with regional air temperature.

title: Ocean circulation changes rather than global warming drove temperature trends across the Miocene Climatic Optimum
abstract: Early-to-Middle Miocene [23 to 13.8 million years ago (Ma)] climates were ∼6° to 9°C warmer than today. Around 16.9 Ma, benthic foraminiferal oxygen isotope (δ 18 O) records suggest pronounced warming, known as the Miocene Climatic Optimum (MCO) onset. However, explaining this putative global warming with carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) forcing faces challenges in terms of timing and forcing magnitude. Our new biomarker-based ocean temperature records, combined with published data, reveal no substantial mean global upper ocean warming across the MCO. Instead, temperature changes differ considerably between sites, with some regions showing cooling. Climate model sensitivity tests indicate that these patterns are best explained by ocean circulation changes, likely due to gateway changes and Antarctic ice sheet variations. This suggests that the MCO signature is better attributed to ocean circulation changes rather than a CO 2 -driven global warming event. The δ 18 O signal therefore represents warmer deepwater sourcing and/or reduced Antarctic glacial volume, resolving the longstanding challenge of explaining MCO warming without a pronounced CO 2 rise.

title: Hidden subsurface suspended sediment export from Greenland's marine‐terminating glaciers
abstract: Abstract Runoff and calved ice volumes from the Greenland Ice Sheet are well constrained, but quantifying the associated suspended sediment flux remains challenging. Here we present near‐terminus observations from three glacierized fjords in southeast Greenland, combining full‐depth turbidity profiles and current velocity from summer 2024 to evaluate sediment export. We identify extensive subsurface sediment plumes from marine‐terminating glaciers which are undetectable using remote sensing approaches and underrepresented in fjord sediment‐core reconstructions. Sediment cores document an exponential increase in sediment accumulation rates from glacier‐distal to glacier‐proximal coring sites. Therefore, the scarcity of sediment cores collected in the immediate vicinity of glacier termini suggests that sediment export from marine‐terminating glaciers has likely been systematically underestimated. Our findings underscore the importance of direct observations for quantifying sediment transport in glacierized fjords and suggest the Greenland Ice Sheet contributes more sediment to ocean margins than previously assumed.

title: Subseasonal forecast improvements from sea ice concentration data assimilation in the Antarctic
abstract: Antarctic sea ice has shifted from its overall increasing trend in the past decades to the recent decline, which attracted attention from the research community. Providing more accurate subseasonal predictions of Antarctic sea ice is critical to managing the accelerating human activities. We demonstrate that by incorporating satellite observations of sea ice concentration with modeling, the subseasonal predictions of Antarctic sea ice can be improved significantly.

title: Holocene forest-line and climate dynamics in the Rondane-Dovre area, S-Norway, inferred from pine ( Pinus sylvestris ) megafossils and pollen data, with the emphasis on the early Holocene and the Holocene thermal maximum (HTM)
abstract: The result of 97 megafossils of pine from the Rondane-Dovre area is here presented. Of these, 84 megafossils are published for the first time. As the regional present forest-lines are situated at varying elevations, the elevations of megafossil finds are adjusted accordingly and thereafter corrected for land uplift before making paleo-ecological inferences. Our findings show that pine established a vertical belt of ca. 250 m around 9.5 ka BP. Around 8–9 ka BP, the pine-forest line reached the Holocene maximum elevations situated ca. 180 m higher than today, indicating that the July mean was warmest in the early Holocene at least 1.2°C warmer than present. Thereafter, pine forests declined and were replaced by the less warmth-demanding birch forests. A comparison with other Fennoscandian paleoecological studies shows that pine immigrated to S-Norway around 10.3 ka BP from the south and the east which is later than the immigration of the more warmth-demanding Hippophaë. This indicates that in Fennoscandia, the Holocene thermal maximum (HTM), at least regarding summer temperatures, was reached in the early Holocene around 9–10 ka BP, a fact that seems overlooked in the ongoing discussion of the timing of HTM. After 8 ka BP, our findings show that colder summers caused decreases in pine pollen production whereas pine-forest-lines were less affected. This shows how temperatures could influence on pollen production and obscure pollen-based reconstructions of past vegetation. During the 8.2 cold event, winter stress prevented pine regeneration. In the period 4.9–1.5 ka BP, the regional pine-forest line descended below the present, probably due to colder climate. Locally, human impact could also have been involved. After 1.5 ka BP, reappearing megafossils could reflect the Medieval warm period. However, data is too scarce to establish elevations of forest-lines.

title: Improved Parameterization of Snow Albedo in WRF/Noah-MP: Methodology Based on Snow Ablation in Upper Yellow River
abstract: Abstract Snow ablation processes have been shown to exert a significant influence on the management of water resources, as well as on the prevention of drought and flood within basin. However, modeling these processes remains challenging due to complex physics and topography. This study develops an improved snow albedo (ISA) scheme for the Noah-MP land surface model that dynamically integrates snow age, depth, and temperature to refine the albedo decay process. We implemented this scheme in WRF model to simulate a severe snow accumulation and ablation event in the Upper Yellow River basin from January to March 2008. Compared to the default Noah-MP (CLASS/BATS) schemes, our improved scheme significantly enhances simulation accuracy. It reduces the mean bias for snow cover fraction (SCF) to 4.19% (from >20%), decreases the surface albedo RMSE by at least 34% (to 0.069), and substantially mitigates the air temperature cold bias, cutting its RMSE by approximately 33.6% (1.1°C). The results demonstrate that a more physical representation of snow albedo is key to improving the surface energy balance and reducing the pervasive cold bias in regional climate simulations over complex terrain. This work provides a validated and effective approach for enhancing snow process modeling in high-altitude regions.

title: Deep learning in the abyss: a stratified Physics Informed Neural Network for data assimilation
abstract: arXiv:2503.19160v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The reconstruction of deep ocean currents is a major challenge in data assimilation due to the scarcity of interior data. In this work, we present a proof of concept for deep ocean flow reconstruction using a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN), a machine learning approach that offers an alternative to traditional data assimilation methods. We introduce an efficient algorithm called StrAssPINN (for Stratified Assimilation PINNs), which assigns a separate network to each layer of the ocean model while allowing them to interact during training. The neural network takes spatiotemporal coordinates as input and predicts the velocity field at those points. Using a SIREN architecture (a multilayer perceptron with sine activation functions), which has proven effective in various contexts, the network is trained using both available observational data and dynamical priors enforced at several collocation points. We apply this method to pseudo-observed ocean data generated from a 3-layer quasi-geostrophic model, where the pseudo-observations include surface-level data akin to SWOT observations of sea surface height, interior data similar to ARGO floats, and a limited number of deep ARGO-like measurements in the lower layers. Our approach successfully reconstructs ocean flows in both the interior and surface layers, demonstrating a strong ability to resolve key ocean mesoscale features, including vortex rings, eastward jets associated with potential vorticity fronts, and smoother Rossby waves. This work serves as a prelude to applying StrAssPINN to real-world observational data.

Seasonal surface melt onset and firn freeze-up across the central Wrangell and St. Elias Mountains
abstract: Mountain snow at high elevations is changing as warming causes more melting and water to linger within it. We use satellite radar images from 2015 to 2024 to track when melting starts and when snow refreezes across the Wrangell and St. Elias Mountains on the border of Alaska and Yukon. We find that melting now reaches nearly all elevations, and water often remains trapped well into fall. Only the highest areas stay fully dry, showing widespread impacts of warming on mountain snowpacks.

title: A standardized permafrost ground temperature collection for Canada 2025
abstract: Ground temperature data is vital for permafrost and climate research yet data is often fragmented. We created a standardized collection of ground temperatures from over 900 sites across Canada. From 42 published and unpublished sources, we manually verified, cleaned and standardized data with a new software tool. This dataset supports permafrost research on a nationwide scale and can help improve models by acting as a reliable benchmark.

title: Generative modelling for multivariate spatio-temporal downscaling of monthly climate fields
abstract: arXiv:2610.19885v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inferring climate fields at higher spatio-temporal resolutions from coarse representations is essential for accessing socioeconomic and environmental impacts. The downscaling of modelled climate fields faces a trade-off between data storage constraints, simulation efficiency, and resolution requirements. While many methods for spatial downscaling have been proposed, joint spatio-temporal downscaling has received comparable little attention. When deriving, for example, daily fields from climate datasets that are available only as monthly averages at coarser spatial resolution, it is highly challenging to faithfully reproduce extreme event statistics and spatiotemporal consistency. To address this task, we introduce a generative machine learning approach, using a diffusion model to jointly downscale monthly temperature and precipitation fields into temporally consistent daily fields at higher spatial resolution. We demonstrate that our approach can generate high-dimensional multivariate climate fields at daily temporal and 0.25{\deg} spatial resolution from monthly input fields at 1{\deg} spatial resolution, exhibiting coherent temporal dynamics and physically plausible spatial structures. In particular, by incorporating a conditional guidance technique, we show that a pre-trained diffusion model can be directly leveraged to efficiently generate daily high-resolution fields conditioned on monthly inputs, without requiring additional fine-tuning or retraining. Our probabilistic approach thus provides an efficient and generalizable framework for spatio-temporal climate downscaling, enabling flexible climate fields generation for climate impact assessments and digital Earth simulator constructions.

title: Hydrological responses to climate change in a central Himalayan basin: insights from snow and glacier runoff modelling
journal: International Journal of River Basin Management
abstract: Assessment of the impacts of climate change on central Himalayan hydrology is vital for the sustainable management of downstream water resources under recent CMIP6 climate projections. We focused on the hydrological processes and water components of the Ghaghara River basin (GRB), particularly on snow- and glacier-melt runoff under projected CMIP6 scenarios. The Spatial Processes in Hydrology (SPHY) model was calibrated and validated for the baseline period (2001–2010), achieving good-to-excellent performance at daily and monthly scales. In the baseline scenario, snow and glacier melt contributed 13.17% and 6.09% of total runoff, respectively. The snowmelt runoff declined by up to 5.49%; however, glacier melt increased by up to 6.13% under the high-emission scenario (SSP5-8.5) compared to the baseline. Rainfall-runoff is expected to increase by ~8% relative to the baseline period. Snowmelt runoff anomalies are expected to decrease after mid-century, particularly under high-emission scenarios, due to reduced snow cover during melt periods. The findings suggest that incorporating climate projections and their associated uncertainties is important for regional water management and planning.

title: Episodic isolation of the Arctic Mediterranean from the North Atlantic during late Pleistocene glacials
abstract: Abstract It has been proposed that the Arctic Ocean and Nordic Seas (“the Arctic Mediterranean”) were not only episodically covered by an ice shelf during late Pleistocene glaciations, but disconnected from the North Atlantic and filled with freshwater. Originally based on the widespread occurrence of marine sediments with intervals barren of 230 Th xs (a function of salinity) and low in cosmogenic 10 Be (interpreted as ice cover), this interpretation is highly debated. Alternative explanations state that sediment pulses could instead have diluted both isotopes. Here, we trace the connection between the Arctic Mediterranean and the North Atlantic using reactive 10 Be/ 9 Be, a water mass tracer resilient to sedimentation variations. We find uniformly low 10 Be/ 9 Be that coincide with the 230 Th xs -minima and more than one order of magnitude below the coeval North Atlantic, consistent with an isolated Arctic Mediterranean. Our findings suggest a highly dynamic coupling between the Arctic Mediterranean and the North Atlantic, opening questions about its impact on global climate.

abstract: Glaciers on the Tibetan Plateau are losing mass, yet their turbulent heat exchange with the atmosphere remains uncertain. We also showed that during a humid heatwave, turbulent heat input rose sharply and accelerated melt, highlighting the need to improve models under extreme conditions.

title: Long-term changes and attribution of lake water levels on the Tibetan Plateau revealed by multisource satellite altimetry data
abstract: ABSTRACT Monitoring Tibetan Plateau (TP) lakes is constrained by harsh environments and methodological limitations. To overcome the limited spatiotemporal coverage of single-mission satellite altimetry and the shortcomings of conventional linear analyses, we integrated CryoSat-2 and Sentinel-3A/B altimetry observations with a multilevel robust anomaly-detection framework to generate water-level time series for 11 representative TP lakes (2010–2026). Seasonal-Trend Decomposition using LOESS (STL) and an XGBoost–SHapley Additive exPlanations(SHAP) framework was subsequently employed to characterize spatiotemporal variations and assess nonlinear associations with five hydrometeorological factors. The generated time series showed strong agreement with in-situ observations (R > 0.94, RMSE: 0.07–0.11 m). Over the 16-year study period, more than 80% of the investigated lakes exhibited sustained water-level increases, with a regional mean rate of 0.27 m yr -1 . However, lake trajectories recent lake trajectories diverged, with some showing accelerated rises and others displaying decelerating or reversed trends. Intra-annual variability also intensified: the mean seasonal amplitude increased by 48.6% (0.17 m) during the last five years. Attribution analysis revealed substantial spatial heterogeneity. While statistical modeling indicated that precipitation (32.5%) and groundwater (21.6%) made the largest regional contributions within the XGBoost framework, individual lakes exhibited predominantly precipitation-dominated, thermal-loss-sensitive, or groundwater-associated response patterns. These contrasting patterns are likely modulated by differences in basin topography, lake morphology, and local geological settings. These findings provide an improved basis for estimating lake-water-storage changes, assessing long-term water-level trends, monitoring overflow and flood hazards, and investigating interactions among lake ecosystems, climate variability, and regional water resources across the TP.

title: EnviFlux (v1.0): a simplified surface flux inversion tool based on four-dimensional variational data assimilation (4D-Var)
abstract: EnviFlux is a low-cost data assimilation tool to estimate trace gas fluxes at the Earth's surface. Data assimilation ideas are often first studied with "toy models", but none exists for flux estimation, hence the purpose of EnviFlux. EnviFlux is described, and then used to show how model error and bias can influence the inferred surface flux features. This is done in two scenarios, one with no prior knowledge of a source/sink pair, and another with prior knowledge in a more realistic situation.

title: Long-Range Distillation: Distilling 10,000 Years of Simulated Climate into Long Timestep AI Weather Models
abstract: arXiv:2512.22814v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Accurate long-range weather forecasting remains a major challenge for AI models, both because errors accumulate over autoregressive rollouts and because reanalysis training datasets provide limited sampling of the slow modes of variability underpinning predictability. Most AI and all numerical weather prediction models are autoregressive, repeatedly applying short-lead forecasts to reach subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) or seasonal lead times, often causing instability and miscalibration. Long-timestep probabilistic models that generate long-range forecasts in a single step offer an alternative, but training on the 40-year reanalysis record leads to overfitting, suggesting orders of magnitude more data are required. We introduce long-range distillation, whereby a long-timestep probabilistic ``student'' model is trained to forecast directly at long-range using a huge synthetic dataset generated by an autoregressive ``teacher'' model. Using the Deep Learning Earth System Model (DLESyM) as teacher, we generate over 10,000 years of simulated climate to train student models across a range of timescales. In perfect-model experiments, the distilled models outperform climatology and approach their teacher's skill while replacing hundreds of autoregressive steps with a single timestep. In the real world, both a diffusion model student fine-tuned on ERA5 and a linear inverse model student with mixed DLESyM-ERA5 training achieve S2S forecast skill competitive with the ECMWF IFS ensemble, with synthetic pre-training providing improvements beyond ERA5-only training. This demonstrates the benefit of synthetic pre-training for both deep learning and classical data-driven methods, and represents the first demonstration that real-world skill can be improved by training on AI-generated synthetic data in volumes far exceeding the observational record.

title: Climatic heterogeneity determines the distribution and resilience of Tibetan Plateau rock glaciers
abstract: Rock glaciers (RGs) are pivotal indicators of mountain permafrost, yet the environmental controls governing their distribution patterns remain poorly understood. Using a generalized boosted model and an inventory of over 40,000 RGs, this study reveals regional shifts in the dominant environmental controls of RG distribution across the Tibetan Plateau. In the westerly-dominated northwest, snow duration days are the primary control, indicating snow as the main ice source; whereas wind speed, overlooked in earlier studies, emerges as the leading driver in the monsoon-influenced southeast. Specifically, wind speeds exceeding 3.2 m·s −1 favor RG occurrence, possibly by enhancing ventilation-induced cooling within coarse blocky layers. Subregional models outperform plateau-wide models by better capturing localized environmental thresholds, underscoring the importance of regionalized approaches for permafrost prediction. Projections further suggest that climatic suitability for RG occurrence remains relatively resilient to future warming scenarios, with implications for the potential role of RGs as hydrological buffers in high-mountain environments.

title: Propagating meteorological uncertainty in physically based mountain snow modeling
abstract: Improving mountain snow prediction requires better representation of meteorological uncertainty. This study generates meteorological ensembles accounting for topography, gauge undercatch, and large-scale atmospheric patterns. Driving a physics-based snow model calibrated using a Large Sample Emulator with these ensembles propagates forcing uncertainty into snow accumulation and melt, producing probablistic estimates for data assimilation and hydrological forecasting.

title: Njord: A Probabilistic Graph Neural Network for Ensemble Ocean Forecasting
abstract: arXiv:2605.15470v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Ocean dynamics are inherently chaotic, yet existing machine learning ocean models produce only deterministic forecasts. We introduce Njord, a probabilistic data-driven model for ocean forecasting, applicable to both global and regional domains. Njord combines a deep latent variable framework with a graph neural network architecture, enabling sampling each forecast step in a single forward pass. We apply Njord globally at 0.25{\deg} resolution and regionally to the Baltic Sea at 2 km resolution. To scale to these large ocean grids we introduce K-means cluster meshes that adapt to irregular sea surface geometry. Experiments demonstrate strong performance on both domains compared to deterministic machine learning baselines, while also providing uncertainty estimates from the sampled ensemble forecasts. On the global OceanBench benchmark, Njord achieves the lowest errors on average across upper-ocean variables when evaluated against real-world observations, with the largest improvements in surface temperature prediction.

title: A Comprehensive Review on Ice Stupa Technology: Artificial Glacier Systems for Climate-Change Adaptation, Water Security and Sustainable Mountain Development in Cold-Arid Regions
journal: Journal of Scientific Research and Reports
abstract: Cold-arid mountain communities depend heavily on seasonal snow and glacier melt, yet climate-driven changes in cryospheric processes are altering the timing and reliability of water availability. This review critically examines ice stupa technology as an artificial glacier system designed to store winter streamflow as ice and release meltwater during the critical spring irrigation period. The review synthesises evidence on the historical development, physical principles, engineering design, hydrological performance, agricultural relevance, ecological implications, socio-economic dimensions, economics, policy relevance and future research needs of ice stupas. The available evidence indicates that ice-stupa performance is governed primarily by meteorological conditions, surface-energy exchange, hydraulic head and cone geometry. Their compact vertical form can delay ablation, while gravity-fed systems enable operation without pumping energy. Recent advances in automated fountain scheduling substantially improve water-use efficiency and reduce operational failures associated with pipe freezing. However, storage remains primarily village-scale, hydrological performance varies considerably between years and economic, ecological and long-term socio-economic outcomes remain insufficiently quantified. Ice stupas therefore function most appropriately as supplementary seasonal water-storage systems rather than substitutes for natural glaciers or large-scale reservoirs. Their effectiveness depends on careful siting, appropriate engineering, reliable monitoring, community participation and integration with broader catchment-management strategies. Future research should prioritise long-term hydrological monitoring, standardised performance assessment, economic evaluation, ecological measurement and climate-sensitive scaling frameworks.

title: Retrieving Tropical Cyclone Intensity from Climate Reanalysis using Deep Learning
abstract: Abstract Traditional methods for improving tropical cyclone (TC) intensity from climate model outputs or projections have primarily relied on either dynamical or statistical downscaling. With recent advances in deep learning (DL) techniques, it is of interest to examine how DL can provide an alternative approach for enhancing TC intensity and structure retrieval from climate data. Using a common DL architecture based on convolutional neural networks (CNN) and a set of key environmental features relevant to TCs, we show that TC intensity and size can be effectively retrieved from climate reanalysis data without requiring super-resolution enhancement as in previous studies, even when applied to coarse-resolution climate data. This approach allows for retrieving TC intensity metrics and size that are dynamically constrained by the data, rather than estimating these quantities independently. Our results highlight that TC intensity and size are governed not only by TC internal processes but also by local environments during TC development for which DL models can learn and capture. The performance of our DL model depends on several factors such as season, the stage of TC development, or ocean basins, with root-mean-square errors ranging from ≈8–10 ms −1 for the maximum 10-m wind, ≈10–13 hPa for minimum central pressure, and ≈13–21 km for the radius of the maximum wind. Although these errors are better than any direct vortex detection or statistical downscaling methods applied to the same data, their wide ranges also suggest that a 0.5°-resolution climate data may contain limited TC information for DL models to learn from, regardless of model optimizations or architectures. Possible improvements and challenges in addressing the lack of fine-scale TC information in coarse-resolution climate reanalysis datasets are discussed.

title: A Graph Neural Network for Global Daily Fire Radiative Power Prediction at Medium-Range Lead Times
abstract: arXiv:2610.11022v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Skillful prediction of biomass-burning activity several days in advance is important for air-quality forecasting and aerosol prediction. Two operational constraints motivate this work. First, the GBBEPx satellite fire radiative power (FRP) product used to initialize NOAA's GEFS-Aerosols is available with about a 1.5-day latency, so each forecast cycle relies on the most recently available, but already outdated, fire observations. Second, these fire inputs are then held fixed throughout the subsequent 5-day operational forecast, or 7 days in the GSL experimental system, effectively assuming no evolution in fire activity. We develop a data-driven model that predicts global FRP one to seven days ahead from the most recent available observations. The model adapts a spatiotemporal graph neural network using reanalysis meteorology, land-cover and vegetation information, recent fire history, and GBBEPx FRP as the training target. It is trained on 2020-2022 data and evaluated for 2023-2024. The model reproduces the global seasonal cycle and substantially outperforms persistence. At 0.1$^\circ$ resolution, mean squared error is reduced by 32% at one-day lead and 43% at seven days in 2023, and by 24% and 40% in 2024. At 1$^\circ$ resolution, the critical success index ranges from 0.32 to 0.60. Detection skill declines only modestly with lead time, whereas intensity skill degrades more rapidly. Large fires are detected reliably, but their radiative power is systematically underestimated. These results demonstrate useful predictability of fire activity several days ahead and identify intensity calibration and small-fire placement as the main remaining challenges before predicted FRP can support operational aerosol forecasts.

title: Glacial lake outburst flood hazard and downstream impacts: lessons from Afghanistan examples
abstract: Abstract Glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) pose a growing risk in high mountain regions as climate-driven glacier retreat accelerates lake expansion and new lake formation. In the Hindu Kush Himalaya, particularly in Afghanistan, triggering processes and GLOF propagation downstream are largely unstudied. This study evaluates two Afghanistan GLOFs (Peshghor 2018; Bam-Tanab 2021) using field observations and satellite imagery, and applies two-dimensional hydrodynamic simulation (BASEMENT-MD with BASEbreach) to the Kunj-Peshghor lake event to assess flood propagation, dam-breach dynamics, and downstream hazards under different scenarios. Both lakes formed and expanded over 33–42 days before catastrophic drainage, triggered by extreme temperatures, rapid-melt, ice-cliff collapse, and englacial tunnel failure. Both impacted Peshghor village downstream. The Kunj-Peshghor lake flood wave produced estimated peak velocities of 9 ms −1 and depths >10 m in confined valleys, associated with peak discharges >170 m 3 s −1 , high turbidity >800 NTU, and channel widening of up to 250 m. Secondary surges caused by temporary river blockages prolonged flooding and amplified downstream impacts. Hazard mapping indicates that ~46% of inundated zones in the Peshghor village fell within high to very high hazard levels, threatening settlements, roads, markets, and agricultural land. These findings provide the first quantitative GLOF propagation modeling for Afghanistan and highlight the need for site-specific monitoring, early warning systems, and mitigation measures. Both GLOFs were caused by the rapid formation and expansion of new lakes. This raises the question about whether current approaches to identifying dangerous lakes, based on remote-sensing of existing lakes are sufficient to detect all dangerous lakes and the associated hazards.

title: Land surface model snow formulation sensitivity and a solar-zenith-angle snow covered area scheme evaluated across the western United States
abstract: Accurate representation of snow water equivalent (SWE) remains a central challenge for land surface and integrated hydrologic models. This work expands the ParFlow-CLM snow model with several new parameterizations, including a formulation that modulates fractional snow covered area (fSCA) by solar zenith angle. I evaluate these parameterizations across 220 site-years from the SNOTEL observation network, spanning three experiments and 58 configurations that represent the major snow parameterization choices in the literature, including three albedo schemes, five rain-snow partitioning methods, and band-separated snow aging formulations. A systematic sensitivity analysis shows that fSCA is the dominant control on SWE prediction accuracy among the tested parameterizations, with fSCA changes producing larger improvements than any tested change to albedo scheme, rain-snow partitioning, or snow aging. Static fSCA corrections improve peak SWE but introduce a trade-off with melt timing. The new solar-zenith-angle-modulated fSCA scheme resolves this trade-off by using seasonal solar geometry to transition between snow-preserving accumulation and snow-exposing ablation conditions. Across all configurations, the SZA-fSCA scheme achieves the best balance of peak accuracy and melt timing (NSE 0.79, melt bias of −1 day), surpassing reanalysis products and default process-model benchmarks and approaching LSTM performance (NSE 0.82 versus 0.86) when combined with forcing bias correction. These advancements provide physics-based snow options for ParFlow-CLM comparable to those in other widely used land surface and snow models. Improved representation of snow water equivalent supports more accurate integrated continental hydrologic simulation over the United States.

title: Review of the Salpausselkä ice‐marginal formations in Finland
abstract: ABSTRACT Extensive Salpausselkä ice‐marginal formations were deposited in southern and eastern Finland during the Weichselian deglaciation. These comprise three major ridges (I, II, and III Salpausselkäs) and their eastern counterparts (Tuupovaara, Koitere, and Pielisjärvi), together forming laterally continuous ice‐marginal formations extending approximately 650 km, with a total mapped length of 1530 km. Among the largest ice‐marginal deposits globally, the Salpausselkäs consist mainly of glaciofluvial sand and gravel, locally interbedded with till. They include ice‐contact deltas, subaqueous fans, sandurs, moraine slabs and ridges, and shoreline deposits, with depositional architecture strongly controlled by ice‐lobe dynamics, meltwater discharge, proglacial water depth, and bedrock topography. In this review, we synthesize the current understanding of the chronology, composition, and depositional environments of the Salpausselkäs, drawing together a substantial body of literature accumulated over the decades, including numerous studies published only in the Finnish language. Uncertainties related to their deposition, as well as topics requiring further investigation, are also discussed.

title: Physical Processes Driving Year-to-Year Surface Temperature Variability Changes in a Warming Climate
abstract: arXiv:2610.19389v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Under anthropogenic greenhouse forcing, climate models project a decrease in year-to-year temperature variability in the mid-to-high latitudes and an increase in the tropics and subtropics. Here, we examine year-to-year temperature variability in the CESM Large Ensemble in concert with an idealized stochastic moist energy balance model (SMEBM) with effective surface heat capacity and local feedback parameter specified based on CESM. We find that the zonal-mean CESM variability change pattern largely persists after filtering out the impact of El Ni\~no. The SMEBM largely captures this change pattern. In the SMEBM, changes in the mid-to-high latitudes are driven by changes in the effective heat capacity due to sea ice retreat, combined with changes in anomalous moist static energy convergence modulated by the polar-amplified time-mean temperature change. The CESM local feedback parameter evolves to be less stabilizing in the low latitudes, which causes tropical and subtropical variability to increase in the SMEBM.

abstract: Preprint under review for ESSD (discussion: open, 0 comments) Flash floods develop quickly, but the records needed to study them are scattered across many sources. We created TORRENT by linking flood reports, rainfall, river flow, drainage-area information, and field measurements across the contiguous United States. It contains 42 466 reported events and 806 ready-to-use case packages, including 21 carefully checked cases. Its open, machine-readable design will help people and artificial intelligence tools study floods and compare prediction methods.

title: Variable Masking for Climate Emulation in ACE
abstract: arXiv:2610.21012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the recent AI Model Intercomparison Project (AIMIP) benchmark, the ACE2.1-ERA5 emulator was shown to underestimate the true near-surface warming trend both during the training period and the out-of-sample extrapolation period. In this work, we present M-ACE2S (Masked-ACE2S), a modified version of the stochastic ACE2S model, which uses variable masking during training and reduces the reliance of M-ACE2S on any single input channel. We show that M-ACE2S improves long-term near-surface air temperature prediction. We also present a novel data normalization strategy called "global mean removal", which, combined with masking, further improves the near-surface temperature forecasts. We show that M-ACE2S outperforms the ACE2S baseline on in-sample data for ERA5 while improving training stability and generalizability of near-surface temperature to unseen forcing when paired with global mean removal.

title: Causal Fingerprints Reveal Hidden Mechanisms in Partially-Observed Dynamical Systems
abstract: arXiv:2610.22286v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In partially-observed dynamical systems, distinct hidden mechanisms can produce similar observable summary statistics while explaining individual events differently. We introduce causal fingerprints: realization-dependent patterns that track how information about a hidden state is revealed through subsequent evolution. Within a prescribed dynamical model, we compare the filtering posterior, based on observations up to a given time, with the smoothing posterior, obtained after adding an expanding window of future observations. We quantify this retrospective information gain using Kullback-Leibler divergence and track its evolution as the future window of observational data expands. The fingerprint reveals both the strength and temporal reach of hidden influence, which can vary across events and their stages. Because the observed trajectory is held fixed while hidden-state inference depends on the candidate model, fingerprints reveal how competing dynamical mechanisms explain the same observations even when selected statistics agree. In linear Gaussian systems, we derive a characteristic fingerprint timescale for the temporal reach of hidden influence. Calibrated surrogates matching the observable mean, variance, and decorrelation time can still produce distinct fingerprints when feedback memory, hidden-noise memory, or hidden forcing timescales are misrepresented. Nonlinear examples reveal mechanism-dependent signatures for extreme bursts, oscillatory variability, and regime switching, including multiplicative instability versus additive forcing, deterministic nonlinear feedback versus state-dependent multiplicative noise, and intrinsic bistability versus hidden double-well forcing. Causal fingerprints therefore provide a time- and event-resolved diagnostic for asking not only whether a model reproduces observed statistics, but how its hidden dynamics explain individual events.

title: Spatiotemporal Assessment of Baltoro Glacier Snow-Cover Dynamics: Relevance to Indus Basin Water Resources and Irrigation
abstract: Glaciers of the Karakoram feed the Upper Indus, whose meltwater supports one of the largest irrigation systems in the world and, through it, the soils and crops of Pakistan. This study assessed the change in snow-covered surface of Baltoro Glacier between 2000 and 2020 and tested its relationship with temperature and precipitation. Landsat 5, 7 and 8 imagery was classified with the Normalized Difference Snow Index (NDSI) in ArcGIS, and climate data (2000-2020) were obtained from NASA POWER (MERRA-2) for the glacier grid cell (35.92° N, 74.30° E; mean elevation 3,627 m). Snow-covered area declined by 9 percentage points between December 2000 and December 2020 and by 13 percentage points between August 2000 and August 2020 (mean 11). Annual loss increased significantly through time (0.041% yr⁻¹; r = 0.79, p < 0.001) and averaged 0.30% yr⁻¹ in 2000-2012 compared with 0.89% yr⁻¹ in 2013–2020. Simple linear regression showed positive but statistically non-significant associations of snow-cover loss with temperature (R² = 0.034, p = 0.43) and precipitation (R² = 0.056, p = 0.30). The modest overall loss is consistent with the Karakoram anomaly and the insulating effect of supraglacial debris, whereas the late-period acceleration warrants monitoring because changes in glacier snow cover may have implications for downstream water resources, including irrigation, soil moisture and salinity management.

title: An abrupt shift towards a hotter and drier climate regime in the Western Eurasian Steppe

title: Introducing a new normalized cryospheric index (NCI) to categorize sub-watersheds on arid environments
abstract: In arid zones, water comes mainly from snow, glaciers and ice-rich permafrost landforms. We introduce the Normalized Cryospheric Index (NCI), which combines ice storage and snow permanence to rank sub-watersheds where no regulatory framework exists. Applied to the Copiapó basin (Atacama, Chile), the NCI identifies the Montosa, Del Potro, Manflas and Estero Come Caballos sub-watersheds as priority targets for sustaining runoff in Chile's national water resources strategy.

title: Collaborative Neural Networks significantly Improve Global Aerosol Retrievals From Multi-Angle Polarimeters
abstract: arXiv:2610.19217v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present the RemoTAP-Hybrid algorithm for global aerosol products retrieved from Multi-Angle Polarimeters (MAP), and apply it to one-year aerosol retrievals from the SPEXone MAP instrument. For the first time, Multiple Collaborated Neural Networks (MCNN) are used to perform global aerosol MAP retrievals over land and ocean. The combined use of MCNN with a full physics inversion in RemoTAP-Hybrid, significantly improves accuracy and computational speed of SPEXone aerosol retrievals. We validate the retrieved Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD), Angstrom Exponent (AE), Single Scattering Albedo (SSA), Absorption AOD (AAOD), Fine mode AOD (FAOD), Coarse mode AOD (CAOD), and fine mode effective radius (reff_fine) with AERONET data. The validation suggests that aerosol retrievals can be further improved when extending the aerosol description to include a fine non-spherical mode. For AOD, the Root-Mean-Square Error (RMSE) is 0.051 (0.037) over land (ocean), while 78.3% (80.8%) of the retrievals are within the requirement formulated by the Global Climate Observing System (GCOS). The RMSE is 0.186 (0.207) for AE, 0.038 (0.044) for SSA, 0.023 (0.014) for AAOD, 0.047 (0.031) for FAOD, 0.043 (0.027) for CAOD, and 0.021 (0.026) for reff_fine over land (ocean). Compared to the current RemoTAP algorithm, RemoTAP-Hybrid shows improved agreement with AERONET for AOD, AE, and FAOD over land and ocean while the number of valid retrievals is increased by 4% (3%) over land (ocean) and the computational time is reduced by 43% (32%). Finally, we present the first global seasonal maps of aerosol optical and microphysical properties and chemical composition from SPEXone.

title: Brief communication: Mass balance of glaciers in the Eastern Hindu Kush from 1979 to 2002 using KH-9 panoramic and SPOT-5 stereo imagery
abstract: In the Hindu Kush region, there is a scarcity of observations on the mass balance of glaciers during the pre-2000 period. Here, using stereo imagery from satellites, we estimate that glaciers in the Eastern Hindu Kush have undergone mass loss at a moderate rate during 1979–2002. This study analyzes the behavior of debris-covered and debris-free glaciers as well as surging and non-surging glaciers. We further discuss individual glaciers and identify the major retreating glaciers in the region.

title: TailWeather: from tail to extremes, a global climatological dataset for machine-learning weather forecasting
abstract: Preprint under review for ESSD (discussion: open, 0 comments) Weather forecasts are mostly judged on ordinary days, not on the rare heatwaves, cold spells, storms, downpours, and droughts that cause most harm. We built a global daily record of such unusual weather over land since 1981 and compared it with reported disasters. Rarer weather was more often linked to harm, but disaster records miss much of the world. Leading artificial intelligence forecasts often missed extremes, especially strong winds, so forecasts need testing on extremes everywhere.

title: NUKLEUS—A First Convection-Permitting Multimodel Ensemble for Germany: Assessment of Future Changes in Temperature and Precipitation Extremes
abstract: Abstract This study analyzes a novel nine-member ensemble of convection-permitting regional climate simulations for Germany to assess projected changes in temperature and precipitation extremes under two future global warming levels, +2 and +3 K. The robustness of the climate change signals within the ensemble is also evaluated to ensure the reliability of the results. Throughout the twenty-first century, temperature-related extremes are projected to intensify, with nighttime extremes showing larger increases than daytime extremes. This amplification of nocturnal warming implies elevated risks to human health and ecosystems. While annual precipitation sums in Germany are projected to change only slightly and are mostly not statistically significant, the frequency and intensity of intense and very extreme precipitation events increase substantially. This change signal is particularly evident in summer, despite a predominantly decreasing seasonal mean rainfall. Such contrasting changes indicate a future characterized by generally drier summers interrupted by heavy rainfall events, with implications for both droughts occurrence and flood risk estimates. Temperature-related extremes show high robustness across almost all of Germany, whereas precipitation-related extremes exhibit greater variability, reflecting stronger natural variability and model uncertainty. The high-resolution simulations reveal added value for temperature-based indices, including more detailed spatial patterns of time averages and changes in specific areas, together with reduced uncertainty as indicated by ensemble spread and signal-to-noise ratios. These new climate model projections offer a robust scientific basis and a high potential for developing adaptation strategies tailored to small-scale landscape units.

title: Investigation of glacier mass balance based on multi-source observation in the Karakoram over the past 25 years
abstract: The “Karakoram Anomaly” — the atypical stability of glaciers in a warming climate—has introduced considerable uncertainty into projections of regional water resources. However, the resilience of this anomaly under sustained climate forcing remains poorly quantified. In this study, multi-source geodetic data (ASTER, NASA DEM, ICESat‑2) were integrated to reassess glacier mass balance across the Karakoram and its sub‑regions between 2000 and 2024. Our results indicate a region‑wide specific mass balance of −0.0386 ± 0.0032 m w.e. a − ¹, with strong spatio-temporal heterogeneity. We document a progressive decay of the Karakoram Anomaly: it was region‑wide before 2010, contracted to the northern and central Karakoram during 2010–2020, and has largely weakened since 2020, persisting only in isolated basins. This evolution is closely associated with summer warming and changes in precipitation. Topography exerts a key control on spatial variability. These findings improve our understanding of the Karakoram anomaly and are of great significance for regional water resources management and disaster prevention under climate change.

title: Analysis of Snow Cover Dynamics in the Beas River Basin during 2019-2021
abstract: Snow is a key component of the Himalayan cryosphere and plays a significant role in water resource availability and hydrological processes. This study examines the characteristics of snow cover in the Beas River Basin using MODIS satellite imagery for the period 2019-2021, with particular emphasis on temporal variations in snow cover and its potential influence on the hydrological cycle. Snow Cover Area (SCA) was estimated for the basin using the improved 8-day snow-cover product (Version 6), Terra-Aqua (MOYDGL06), generated from the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) sensor. In addition, snow-cover maps were developed from the MODIS observations to analyse the spatial distribution and temporal variability of snow cover across the Beas River Basin. During the study period, SCA in the region varied from 41% (November 2020) to 90% (February 2019). SCA and total precipitation showed declining trends at rates of 2.1 km² and 47.3 cm, respectively, while the average temperature increased from 2019 to 2021 at a rate of 0.14°C. However, during 2019-2021, SCA declined at a higher rate of 19.21 km² and total precipitation decreased at a rate of 28.6 cm. In contrast, the mean temperature increased at a higher rate of 0.40°C. The study indicates that SCA and precipitation declined more rapidly during 2019-2021. The findings suggest that climate change may be an important factor influencing the observed trends in SCA, precipitation, and mean temperature. The observed SCA trend was also found to be consistent with the climatic parameters. The study examines SCA variability from January to December.

title: Threat and action under strain: Risk Perception Shapes Heat Protective Behavior in the Context of Differing Physical and Mental Health
abstract: Heat can adversely affect both mental and physical health and increase mortality risk. Heat-related deaths are an increasing global phenomenon, particularly during heat waves or sudden temperature increases, before acclimatization can take place. For effective prevention, it is important to identify predictors of heat protection intentions and behaviors. To address the often-neglected risk that heat poses to mental health, we have developed a multidimensional questionnaire to measure heat-related risk perception. It assesses negative affect caused by heat, perceived probability of being affected by heat, and expected consequences of unprotected heat exposure. We examined the scale's relationship with heat protection intention and behavior, as well as whether mental or physical strain negatively moderated this relationship. Self-efficacy and health literacy were additional exogenous variables. A total of 1,803 adults in Germany participated in the study. The data were evaluated using structural equation modeling. After minor adjustments, the measurement model showed a fair fit. All factors of heat-related risk perception, self-efficacy, and the intention to protect oneself from heat were significantly related to heat protection behavior. Negative moderation by physical or mental strain was not detected. The results suggest that the affective factor of heat-related risk perception (e.g., “I feel afraid when I think about heat”), the intention to protect oneself, and self-efficacy are particularly decisive in determining whether people take protective measures against heat. Communication strategies that increase the emotional salience of heat hazards, which are supplemented by programs that specifically strengthen self-efficacy, could effectively elicit behavioral change in physically and mentally inconspicuous and strained populations.

title: Heterogeneous effects of climate change on real GDP per capita: evidence from selected MENA countries and Türkiye
abstract: The Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region is highly exposed to climate risks, but the economies considered in this study differ substantially in their resource structures and sectoral composition. It therefore remains unclear whether a single regional panel average can adequately reflect the relationship between climate change and real gross domestic product (GDP) per capita across these countries. This study examines this relationship using an 11-country panel covering selected MENA countries and Türkiye over the period 1995–2024, with particular attention to Gulf-non-Gulf and country-level variation. The climate variables were the temperature anomaly, the squared temperature anomaly, and the Standardized Precipitation-Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI), with real GDP per capita as the dependent variable. The Cross-Sectionally Augmented Autoregressive Distributed Lag (CS-ARDL) model was employed as the baseline estimator to account for cross-sectional dependence and slope heterogeneity, with Common Correlated Effects Mean Group (CCEMG) and Driscoll-Kraay estimates used as complementary checks. Full-panel results show no strong and consistent average relationship between the climate variables and real GDP per capita across estimators. Subsample estimates suggest a possible negative temperature pattern in the non-Gulf group, but the corresponding marginal effects are not statistically significant at the 5% level and the pattern is not reproduced in additional sensitivity checks. Formal tests do not indicate a statistically significant difference between Gulf and non-Gulf temperature responses. Additional full-panel robustness specifications do not materially alter this conclusion. The study contributes by examining the relationship at the full-panel, subgroup, and country levels. The results suggest that regional averages may conceal some variation across countries and groups, although the small subgroup sizes limit inference and these patterns require confirmation in larger samples. Policy assessment in the region should therefore take country-level conditions into account rather than rely on a single regional average. The findings are also relevant to the broader objectives of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 8 and SDG 13.

abstract: This study proposes a performance-based method to improve WRF climate simulation evaluation by addressing uncertainty in selecting scheme combinations. The method gives greater importance to difficult-to-simulate variables, such as precipitation and wind speed. Tested in two contrasting climate regions, it identified interpretable and well-performing model settings compared with equal weighting and established statistical weighting methods, including in the independent extreme-year test.

title: Unmasking Compensating Errors in Numerical Weather Models: A Process-Additive Neural Network Approach
abstract: arXiv:2610.19772v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work introduces a Process Additive Neural Network (PANN) framework to disentangle compensating biases in atmospheric models, where errors in different physical processes can offset each other and obscure their origins. Using a single-column model, each PANN branch represents the tendency error associated with a separate physical process, and the summed branch outputs approximate the total error relative to a reference tendency. Once trained successfully, the branch outputs are expected to provide process-level error attributions and, when averaged, estimates of process-level bias. Initial experiments focus on cloud-related processes in OpenIFS SCM case studies, where cloud and convection tendencies are strongly coupled and compensation is difficult to diagnose using standard approaches. The aim is not to replace human interpretation of physical processes, but to extend it to regimes where model complexity, process interaction, and compensating errors make direct diagnosis difficult. By providing a physically structured form of machine-learning interpretability, PANN can help connect complex model behaviour with process-level explanations. This work supports both improved understanding of compensating errors and the development of more physically consistent weather and climate models.

title: High-level, efficient ocean modeling at all scales with Oceananigans
abstract: arXiv:2502.14148v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We describe the user interface, governing equations, and numerical methods underpinning the ocean modeling software called "Oceananigans". Oceananigans development has been led by the Climate Modeling Alliance as part of a larger effort to build a trainable climate model with quantifiable uncertainty. Notably, Oceananigans is written in the Julia programming language, is optimized for GPUs, and can efficiently simulate all scales of ocean motion ranging from millimeter-scale turbulence in a small box to planetary-scale ocean circulation. We argue that this combination of capabilities is enabled by a design that combines a basic, easy-to-optimize, GPU-friendly structured finite volume algorithm exposed behind a high-level, programmable user interface. This design negotiates a dual mandate for highest-possible performance (to support state-of-the-art applications) and enhanced accessibility (to facilitate adoption and development). The dual mandate aims ultimately to accelerate the progress of Earth system science.

title: Cosmic Rays as an Interdisciplinary Earth Observation Tool: From Particle Physics and Atmospheric Processes to Geosciences and Urban Science
abstract: arXiv:2601.19265v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The exploration of cosmic rays, which are high-energy particles originating from space and the atmosphere, has historically been associated with particle physics and astrophysics. In the last 20 years, these particles have evolved into valuable tools for observing Earth's systems. This review compiles the use of cosmic rays in three primary areas: (1) particle physics and atmospheric processes, which include cosmic- ray-induced cascades, ionization, and their impact on atmospheric chemistry and radiation; (2) geosciences, where cosmogenic radionuclides assist in the dating of geological materials and cosmic-ray neutrons are used for large-scale monitoring of soil moisture and snow water equivalents; and (3) urban science, where cosmic- ray muons are employed for non-invasive subsurface imaging and, when paired with distributed sensors, serve as the basis for smart city monitoring. This review places particular emphasis on integrating these methods with remote sensing and geographic information systems (GIS), which helps close the persistent scale gap between point measurements and satellite observations, thereby enabling three-dimensional digital representations of subsurfaces. This review concludes by discussing data standards, their integration into operational Earth observation workflows, and future research directions.
