title: KNOU-Flood: Advancing global streamflow forecasting with lead-aware probabilistic machine learning
abstract: arXiv:2610.20640v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Global streamflow forecasting supports flood preparedness, yet data-driven models trained on reanalysis lose skill when driven by operational forecasts, increasingly so with lead time. AIFL addresses this shift with a two-stage transfer-learning recipe and a deterministic LSTM, but it feeds one forecast lead time into the whole input window and gives no uncertainty. We ask how far this open recipe can be extended without changing its recurrent core. KNOU-Flood keeps a single-layer LSTM and the two-stage training and changes the information around it: a longer input window (424 days), lead-aware forecast inputs, GraphCast as a second forecast source next to ECMWF HRES, and a latent-noise ensemble trained with the fair CRPS. We compare against a re-implementation of the AIFL recipe (its code is not public) under identical data, stations, splits and metrics. Our contributions are threefold. First, over three seeds and 2,099 test basins (2021-2023), KNOU-Flood reaches a median KGE' of 0.65 at LT1 and 0.48 at LT10 against 0.62 and 0.34, with significant gains at all ten lead times under two scoring protocols, also against a 1024-unit baseline and on held-out basins (one seed each). Second, identical weights give an LT10 KGE' of 0.18 or 0.34 depending on how forecasts are fed, so much of the lead-time decay reported for AIFL is an input-protocol effect; the probabilistic head contributes most to the gain, followed by the raw GraphCast channels, the longer window and mixed fine-tuning. Third, the ensembles reach lower CRPS than probabilistic versions of the baseline, are nearly calibrated with inference-time dropout, and detect 1.5- and 2-year floods better than all baselines; the benefit for rarer floods depends on the seed, and an exploratory tail-weighted variant improves 10-year and larger events. KNOU-Flood is a controlled extension of an open recipe, not a new architecture.

Can we define climate by means of an ensemble? A tale of time scales of convergence
abstract: Climate and its change is of central importance to science and human society in general. However, it appears to us that a satisfactory definition of climate has not yet appeared in the literature. We attempt to introduce one which is based on an ensemble of realizations and satisfies uniqueness. Within this framework, it also attends to different time scales of relevance, a well-established treatment of which is the main novelty of our work.

title: From concept to action: Driving impact through responsible research practices in the International Polar Year 2032–2033 An early career perspective
abstract: by Samuel G. Hartharn-Evans, Chloe Nunn, Amy Macfarlane, Natalia Banega, Anna Belcher, Radiance Calmer, Svenja Holste, Louise Mercer, Ningning Sun, M. A. J. van Soest, Zoe Wright Regions at the poles are warming at rates two to four times higher than the global average, driving profound environmental, societal, and geopolitical changes. As Polar Early Career Researchers with careers extending into and beyond the 5th International Polar Year in 2032–2033, we have a responsibility to shape research practices that are impactful, ethical, and sustainable. We argue that current definitions of research impact often prioritize narrow, quantifiable metrics, overlooking cultural, environmental, and long-term consequences. Building on interdisciplinary workshops held in 2025 at the Polar Early Career World Summit (USA) and the Centre for Ecology and Hydrology (UK), this paper redefines research impact for polar science and presents tangible action for integrating responsible practices ahead of the next IPY. We outline priorities across three levels: 1) individual researchers, who should practice reflexivity, promote interdisciplinarity, and implement environmentally responsible methods; 2) regional and national institutions, which must provide equitable funding, training, and inclusive protocols; 3) international IPY planning bodies, which should strengthen communication, publish guidelines, and implement regulations to prevent exploitative practices. Our call to action emphasizes collaboration, transparency, and improved impact evaluation frameworks to ensure that polar research delivers societal and environmental benefits while minimizing unintended consequences. This vision begins now and extends beyond the IPY, offering a roadmap for responsible polar science.

title: Strategic Governance of AI Models in Earth Science
abstract: arXiv:2610.10560v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI foundation models pretrained on weather and climate data are increasingly fine-tuned to Earth science tasks well beyond weather forecasting. Their development and adoption are outpacing the scientific community's ability to evaluate them. These models are judged almost entirely by benchmark skill metrics, which measure how closely a forecast reproduces a reference product but not whether a model represents the physical processes governing the system it predicts. Forecast skill and physical reliability are therefore distinct properties. The distinction is most consequential under the nonstationary conditions of a changing climate for which these models were never trained. We identify five priorities for the physical evaluation of AI models in Earth science from task-specific emulators to foundation models, spanning training data, fine-tuning, behavioral testing, mechanistic interpretability, and output validation. We recommend three activities for the coming decade: 1) open AI-ready evaluation datasets, 2) a shared reporting standard for physics-based evaluation, and 3) a dedicated research program on the safety of these models.

title: Climate changes in hydrometeorological parameters of the Varzob river basin in the period 1980–2020
abstract: Introduction. Climate of Tajikistan is shaped by geographic location, complex topography, elevation, atmospheric circulation, and surface characteristics. It is marked by aridity, intense heat, and strong seasonal variation in temperature, humidity, precipitation, and solar radiation. Average annual temperatures range from +17 °C in the south to −6 °C and below in the east; absolute extremes reach −63 °C (Eastern Pamirs) and +48 °C (southwest). Annual precipitation varies from 70-160 mm in lowland and highland deserts to over 1800 mm in the central part of the country. The study examines temperature and precipitation changes (1991-2018) and snow cover dynamics (2005-2020) on the southern slopes of the Gissar Range. The analysis covers changes in meteorological conditions and their impact on the hydrological regime of the Varzob River over two periods: 1981-2000 and 2001-2020. Purpose of the research. To determine changes in meteorological conditions of the Varzob River basin and their impact on the river's hydrological regime over the last two decades of the 20th century (1981-2020) and the first two decades of the 21st century (2001-2020). Materials and Methods. Meteorological data from the Agency for Hydrometeorology of Tajikistan (TMS-84 monthly records) were used. Data were processed in MS Excel; trends were identified by the least square’s method using linear equations (y = ax + b) for temperature and precipitation, and a four-variable polynomial trend (y = ax⁴ + bx³ + cx² + dx + f) for river discharge. Terrain analysis was performed using SRTM imagery and QGIS. Results. 1. In 2001-2020 vs. 1981-2000, mean annual temperature rose by 0.3 °C in Dushanbe, 0.8 °C in Khushyary, and 1.5 °C in Maikhura; at Anzob it decreased by −0.1 °C. 2. Mean annual precipitation for 1981-2020: Anzob – 455.7 mm, Maikhura – 1057.2 mm, Khushyary – 1263.7 mm, Dushanbe – 598.9 mm. A decreasing precipitation trend was observed throughout the Varzob Gorge. 3. Seasonal precipitation (1981-2020): Anzob – 459.3 mm, Maikhura – 1059 mm, Khushyary – 1263.6 mm, Dushanbe – 604.9 mm. In highland areas ~70% of annual precipitation falls in winter and spring; in the basin interior – 75%; in Dushanbe – 80%. 4. Mean annual discharge of the Varzob River: 47.4 m3/s (1981-2000) and 48.9 m3/s (2001-2020), an increase of 1.5 m3/s. 5. The correlation between annual precipitation and mean annual temperature is very weak at all stations (strongest at Anzob, r = 0.025). The strongest precipitation–runoff correlation is between Khushyary station and Dakhana post (r = 0.582); the weakest temperature–runoff correlation is between Maikhura station and Dakhana post (r = −0.239). Resume. Analysis of long-term hydrometeorological data shows that in 2001-2020, compared with 1981-2000, mean annual temperature and river discharge tended to increase, while annual precipitation declined. Interannual correlation between precipitation and temperature is very weak across the basin; the precipitation–discharge correlation is stronger than the temperature–discharge correlation. Suggestions for practical applications and directions for future research. The findings can be applied to climate change research, glaciology, snow cover assessment, water resource management, and regional climate studies.

title: Comparison of data-driven and numerical weather prediction models for rainfall nowcasting in major cities of Bangladesh
abstract: by Sumia Akter, Jayeef Rahman Muaz, Rabiul Awal Flood-prone Bangladesh requires accurate short-term rainfall prediction, yet conventional numerical weather prediction (NWP) models remain computationally intensive and regionally limited in skill. This study evaluates and compares four deep learning (DL) architectures — Simple Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Stacked LSTM, Bidirectional LSTM (BiLSTM), and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) — against the physics-based Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model for one-hour-ahead rainfall forecasting across six climatologically diverse stations in Bangladesh. Each model was trained independently per station using hourly ERA5 reanalysis data spanning 2018–2024, and performance was assessed using both regression and binary detection metrics. Across the full test period, Simple LSTM achieved the strongest overall performance, explaining approximately 88% of ERA5 rainfall variance with the lowest prediction errors, while GRU produced nearly comparable results. Performance was consistently stronger at wetter stations such as Chittagong and Sylhet than at drier northwestern stations such as Rajshahi and Rangpur, where class imbalance and rainfall intermittency limited model skill. Event-category analysis across 10 WRF simulation events — spanning extreme, moderate, and weak rainfall regimes — showed that DL models demonstrated closest agreement with ERA5 reference values during extreme events, while skill declined notably during weak events due to near-zero rainfall conditions. WRF exhibited systematic overestimation, temporal displacement of peak rainfall, and strongly negative R² values across all event categories and stations. A Friedman test confirmed statistically significant differences in RMSE ranks among the four DL architectures (χ² = 10.60, p = 0.014), with a Nemenyi post-hoc test showing Simple LSTM significantly outperformed Stacked LSTM (p = 0.0095).

title: Shifting climate in Caribbean tropical forests: Long-term trends at La Selva (Costa Rica) and El Verde (Puerto Rico)
abstract: by Alonso Ramírez, Marcelo Ardón, Pavel García, Nicholas S. Marzolf, David Genereux Climate change is altering ecosystems worldwide, but long-term, site-level hydroclimatic responses remain comparatively under-documented in many tropical regions. We analyzed long-term air and water temperature, precipitation, and stream water level data from two active Caribbean research sites: La Selva Research Station, Costa Rica, and El Verde Field Station, Puerto Rico. Our goal was to assess long-term hydroclimatic trends and changes in extreme events using continuous monitoring from automatic and manual sensors. Long-term records show a mean daily temperature of 25.1°C (1992–2024, range: 19.5-29.6°C) at La Selva and 23.6°C (2000–2024, range: 17.7-28.2°C) at El Verde. Mean annual precipitation is 4166 mm at La Selva (1983–2024) and 3635.8 mm at El Verde (1975–2024). We found a decadal warming trend of 0.29°C at both locations. The El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) influenced air temperature at El Verde, where La Niña (+0.02°C day −1 , 95% CI: 0.002–0.042) phase was associated with higher daily temperatures, but had no detectable effect on air temperature at La Selva. A significant increase in the frequency of extreme temperature events (defined as exceeding the 95 th , 97 th , and 99 th percentiles) was observed at both sites. Using the 95 th percentile and a fitted generalized linear model, both locations had ~8 extreme temperature events per year in the beginning and increased to ~35 events per year in 2024. Changes in precipitation extremes were site-specific and differed between wet and dry metrics. La Selva showed an increase in wet extremes (heavy precipitation), with 99 th percentile rainfall exceedances rising from ~1 event per year (1983–1985) to 6 per year in 2024. In contrast, El Verde showed no significant increase in heavy-precipitation events, but exhibited an increase in dry extremes (dry days th percentile at La Selva and 95 th percentile at El Verde), with estimated durations above these extreme thresholds roughly doubling over the study period. Overall, our study shows an increasing frequency of extreme events, both wet and dry, at these two Caribbean protected locations. These findings suggest important and distinct regional changes in climate over the region, with important consequences for ecosystem conservation and management.

title: Extensive glacier loss in the coterminous United States
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: Glaciers populate the mountain ranges of the western conterminous United States and despite their importance to alpine hydrology, their area and volume change have never been comprehensively evaluated. Our study shows that since the mid-twentieth century about one-quarter of the glaciers have disappeared and the overall area and volume are reduced by one-third. The pattern of glacier shrinkage suggests most glaciers in the conterminous United States are largely maintained by local topographic influences due to their small size. These results improve our understanding of evolving high alpine hydrology and importance to ecosystem processes.

title: Glacier change at the ISM-MLW transition: multi-decadal evidence of spatial heterogeneity from the Sara Umga watershed, western Himalaya
abstract: This study presents a multi-decadal assessment of glacier change in the Sara Umga Watershed (SUW), between the Parvati and Chandra basins. The region receives a majority of its annual precipitation from Indian Summer Monsoon (ISM) and a comparatively lower share contributed by winter Mid Latitude Westerlies (MLW). Using multi-temporal satellite data, we quantify changes in glacier length, area, surface velocity, elevation, debris cover, ice cliff dynamics, and high-faltitude lakes, supplemented by long-term climate trend analysis. A total of 54 glaciers (>0.05 km 2 ) were mapped, covering 128.38 ± 2.98 km 2 in 2024, of which 24.84 ± 1.15 km 2 comprised debris-covered ice. Between 1994 and 2024, total glacier area declined by 4.54 ± 0.04 km 2 (0.15 ± 0.001 km 2 yr −1 ), while debris cover expanded to 24.84 ± 1.15 km 2 (0.37 ± 0.09 km 2 yr −1 ). Frontal retreat rates for the five major glaciers ranged from ∼12 to 26.2 m yr −1 . The largest glacier, Sara Umga (GL01), exhibited a mean surface velocity of ∼23.4 m yr −1 . Elevation-change analysis reveals pronounced spatial heterogeneity in glacier thinning, with maximum surface lowering concentrated in the lower, debris-covered ablation zone (3900–4400 m a.s.l.; −1.22 ± 0.95 to −1.67 ± 0.39 m yr −1 , locally exceeding −3.0 m yr −1 ), diminishing thinning at mid-elevations, and near-equilibrium conditions across the accumulation area of GL01 (−0.07 ± 0.54 to 0.06 ± 0.33 m yr −1 ). Zones of higher thinning and flow attenuation coincide with dense ice-cliff and lake development, indicating strong melt-dynamics coupling. Climate analysis (1901–2024) shows significant winter warming (0.01 °C yr −1 ) and declining Mid-Latitude Westerly (MLW) dominated winter precipitation (−0.160 mm yr −1 ), alongside increasing pre- (0.354 mm yr −1 ) and post-monsoon (0.070 mm yr −1 ) precipitation. These findings demonstrate that changes in debris-covered Himalayan glaciers cannot be inferred from frontal retreat alone. Instead, coupled changes in thickness, velocity, surface morphology, and climate trends govern long-term glacier response and hence should be studied alongside.

title: Study of Snow Cover Characteristics According to the Data of Meteorological Stations of Western Kazakhstan in the Context of Global Climate Change
abstract: In the Republic of Kazakhstan, runoff in lowland rivers is 90% determined by snowmelt. Therefore, assessing snow reserves in a changing climate is of great scientific and applied importance. This work aims to assess how global climate change affects snow cover characteristics in Western Kazakhstan in the Caspian Sea basin. For the first time, we conducted a comprehensive assessment of snow cover depth, water equivalent, and snow cover duration in the drainage basin. We used statistical analysis of data from 50 meteorological stations for the period 1950–2024. Only data from 14 meteorological stations in the Mugalzhar lowlands (north of the Aktobe region) and on the Podural plateau (north of the West Kazakhstan region), where errors did not exceed 2–4%, were suitable for climate studies. The results showed an increase in average snow height by 3 cm, a decrease in maximum height by 4 cm, and a 17-day reduction in the duration of stable snow cover. However, these trends are not statistically significant (the coefficient of determination is 0.02–0.24), and their values fall within the statistical error. The calculated Pearson and Spearman indicators confirm a statistical relationship between individual global and regional climate indicators (correlation coefficients of 0.23–0.40 at the significance level p = 0.03). However, most snow cover indicators show no statistical dependence: correlation coefficients range from −0.02 to 0.20, with p = 0.30–0.90. The results obtained indicate a random, stochastic nature of the long-term dynamics of depth, water equivalent, and duration of snow cover in the region under study.

title: Past moisture and vegetation conditions at Lake Aura, Norway using n -alkanes and pollen
abstract: Wetlands are valuable paleoenvironmental archives where pollen and n -alkane samples can be collected and used to reconstruct local vegetation patterns and hydrological conditions. However, the impact of local environmental heterogeneity on n -alkanes specifically remains poorly constrained. To address this, we apply a combined n -alkane and pollen approach which allows for a more nuanced reconstruction. In this study, we analyze three separate peat cores around Lake Aura, a high-altitude lake in central Norway, to reconstruct the Holocene vegetation and hydrological development. The area has extensive evidence of successive archaeological activity, and human impacts on vegetation are considered. Our records show a general pattern of arboreal dominance, but with increasing percentages of grassy vegetation towards the Late Holocene, possibly associated with the onset and intensification of pastoralism. Although pollen and n -alkane records broadly converge, intervals where the n -alkane wood/grass ratio rises while the arboreal pollen declines show that the proxies capture different aspects of vegetation change, refining the overall reconstruction. Our study demonstrates the value of combining pollen with molecular markers for reconstructing Holocene vegetation and moisture patterns, and we highlight the broader potential of this tandem approach for refining paleoenvironmental reconstructions in heterogeneous landscapes.

title: PrecipCorrDiff: A Deep Learning Framework for Generating 0.0625$^\circ$ High-Resolution IMD Gridded Precipitation Data
abstract: arXiv:2610.19994v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-resolution precipitation datasets are essential for weather forecasting, hydrological modeling, and climate risk assessment, yet observation-based gridded products often lack the spatial detail required for regional applications. Here we present PrecipCorrDiff, a diffusion-based downscaling framework built by modifying the original corrector diffusion based archetecture that incorporates a customized loss function and a multi-scale residual generation strategy to improve the precipitation especially the representation of extremes. PrecipCorrDiff generates 0.0625{\deg} resolution India Meteorological Department (IMD) precipitation fields from 0.25{\deg} gridded data while preserving precipitation statistics and reconstructing fine-scale spatial variability. Validation against independent IMD station observations, comparing the proposed framework with the SRGAN-based model and the original CorrDiff model, indicates that the proposed framework substantially improves the representation of spatial precipitation patterns, rainfall intensity distributions, and extreme rainfall events, while eliminating the systematic negative bias present in the previously developed SRGAN-based model. Across four climatologically distinct homogeneous Indian monsoon regions, PrecipCorrDiff reproduces observed precipitation characteristics with near-zero spatial bias, demonstrating the potential of diffusion-based downscaling for generating physically consistent, high-resolution precipitation datasets for hydrological, meteorological, and climate applications.

title: Improved Precipitation Variability in the Community Atmosphere Model through Implementation of a Neural-Network Deep Convection Scheme
abstract: arXiv:2610.20405v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conventional deep convection schemes remain a primary source of uncertainty in global climate models, yet replacing them with data-driven alternatives while maintaining physical consistency and numerical stability is an open challenge. We present a hybrid configuration of the Community Atmosphere Model version 6 (CAM6), in which a fully connected deep neural network replaces the Zhang-McFarlane deep convection scheme (ZM), while radiation, turbulence, and other cloud processes are left unchanged. The network is trained on output from a storm-resolving global model - the global System for Atmospheric Modeling (gSAM) - using a coarse-graining approach to derive subgrid-scale convective fluxes and tendencies. This data-driven parameterization is ported to CAM6 and found to run stably for more than a decade while conserving energy and moisture. It produces a broadly realistic climatology without retuning the remaining parameterizations. Relative to the default Zhang-McFarlane scheme, the neural network parameterization substantially improves some long-standing model deficiencies. In particular, the biases in light precipitation and extreme precipitation are markedly reduced, and the diurnal cycle of tropical land precipitation shifts from a spurious midday peak over many regions to the observed late-afternoon peak. These results support targeted ML-based convection schemes as a viable path toward reducing systematic model errors in next-generation climate models.

title: Quantitative Reconstruction of Late Miocene Monsoon‐Driven Climate and Hydrology in the Himalayan Foreland, Nepal
abstract: Abstract The Late Miocene was a critical interval in the evolution of the South Asian monsoon system and the Himalayan foreland. This study presents a quantitative paleoclimatic reconstruction based on fossil leaf assemblages from the Lower (10.5–9.2 Ma) and Middle (9.2–7.0 Ma) Siwalik sediments of the Daldale section, western Nepal, using the Climate Leaf Analysis Multivariate Program (CLAMP). The reconstructed mean annual temperatures are 22.2 ± 2.3°C for the Lower Siwalik and 21.5 ± 2.3°C for the Middle Siwalik, with corresponding cold month mean temperatures of 15.4 ± 3.3°C and 15.0 ± 3.3°C. Mean annual precipitation ranges from 228 ± 48 to 238 ± 48 cm, and the annual vapor pressure deficit remains close to 6 ± 2 hPa, indicating persistently warm and humid monsoon‐influenced conditions throughout the study interval. Although several climatic variables exhibit coherent directional trends, including slightly lower temperatures, reduced rainfall concentration during the wettest months, and subtle changes in seasonal moisture availability in the Middle Siwalik, these differences largely overlap within the uncertainties of the CLAMP reconstructions. Consequently, the Daldale record indicates broad climatic stability rather than a major climatic transition between the Lower and Middle Siwalik intervals within the studied section. The study provides the first quantitative paleoclimatic benchmark for the Daldale Siwalik succession and demonstrates that climatic responses within the Himalayan foreland were spatially heterogeneous, with western Nepal maintaining persistently humid conditions despite broader regional environmental changes.

title: On the theoretical limitations of joint inversion for basal slipperiness and effective viscosity in ice-flow models
abstract: In this study, we investigate the ability to extract information about ice viscosity at the same as basal slipperiness in the inversion procedure of large-scale ice-sheet models. This is an essential part of the initialisation of many large-scale computational ice-sheet models. However, there is a lack of consensus on whether a joint inversion is possible to determine these fields. We present a theoretical framework to better understand the factors influencing the retrieval.

title: Can AI Forecast the Extremes? Evaluating Probabilistic Weather Models on Tropical Cyclones
abstract: arXiv:2610.22077v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Weather prediction is undergoing an important shift, with data-driven AI models outperforming leading numerical weather prediction systems on average at a fraction of the computational cost. Yet, whether this success extends to extreme events remains contested. Earlier evaluations have exposed important shortcomings, but have largely focused on deterministic models and metrics, leaving the capabilities of the latest probabilistic models less understood. We conduct an extensive benchmark of tropical cyclone forecasting, comparing GenCast, FourCastNet 3, and FGN with ECMWF's operational physics-based ensemble, IFS-ENS. We develop a suite of probabilistic metrics and diagnostic analyses to assess cyclone tracking, intensity biases, uncertainty, and the wind-pressure relationship that characterizes storm structure. We find that, despite remaining limitations in intensity and ensemble spread, leading AI models substantially outperform IFS-ENS in cyclone tracking: FGN achieves better probabilistic location scores for 90% of evaluated storms in 2025. Further analyses reveal model-specific failure modes and suggest a lingering influence of pretraining data, pointing to opportunities for targeted improvement. Nonetheless, these results suggest that AI models are capable of capturing physical relationships that remain predictive well beyond typical weather conditions, motivating further investigation into how these capabilities emerge and how to strengthen them.

title: Temperature sensitivity of snow viscoplasticity: Evidence from controlled creep experiments
abstract: Snow slowly compacts under its own weight, and this process depends strongly on temperature, but past estimates vary widely. We developed a device to precisely control temperature and tested the same snow sample under different conditions. We found two distinct temperature regimes and a stronger sensitivity than assumed in existing snowpack models, improving how snow compaction is represented.

title: High-performance geodynamics on GPUs using  the PETSc CUDA backend (GAUZZ v1.0.0)
abstract: Geodynamic simulations of mantle flow repeatedly solve the Stokes equations at high memory and computational cost. We developed a Stokes solver for graphics processing units by coupling two open-source libraries. A single graphics processing unit solved the Stokes equations 6–11 times faster than a 32-core central processor, with the same accuracy. Two units further shortened the solution time of large problems. The doubled memory extended the maximum size of three-dimensional simulations.

Through implementing thread-block indexing, minimizing Central Processing Unit and Graphics Processing Unit communication, and an parallel framework, we demonstrate speedups: 556.5× faster offline performance for the Heterogeneous Interface advection solver and 20.5× acceleration in coupled simulations.

title: Adaptive observation weighting in TCKF1D-Var for  ground-based multi-sensor thermodynamic retrievals  prior to nocturnal heavy precipitation over China
abstract: This study presents an adaptive observation-weighting scheme for thermodynamic profile retrievals from ground-based microwave radiometers and Mie–Raman lidars. The method dynamically estimates observational contributions during the retrieval process, replacing the commonly used static weighting assumption. Evaluation using 107 heavy-precipitation cases shows improved retrieval accuracy, particularly for atmospheric moisture profiles.

title: MONKI: a three-dimensional Monte Carlo simulator for transfer of polarised light in planetary atmospheres
abstract: We present MONKI (Monte Carlo KNMI), an accurate and efficient Fortran radiative transfer code for simulating total and polarised sunlight in 3D planetary atmospheres. Its novelty is the derivation of Monte Carlo equations for the transfer of polarised light, fully accounting for polarisation-dependent scattering directions. This formulation gives reliable convergence even for optically thick, strongly polarising atmospheres, supporting observations of Earth, Venus, or any other planet.

title: Process-based evaluation of green roof models for assessment of heat mitigation efficacy in WRF (v4.3.1) and EnergyPlus (v8.6.0)
abstract: Green roofs can help cool cities, but models must represent them accurately to quantify this potential. Yet few studies evaluate green roof models against real data. We evaluated two versions of EcoRoof, the green roof module in EnergyPlus, and a green roof option for WRF (Weather and Research Forecasting model) using measurements from London, Ontario. EcoRoof generally matched observed heat fluxes, surface temperature, and soil moisture, while WRF overestimated heat and underestimated cooling.

title: Towards high-fidelity simulations of coastal submesoscale  baroclinic instabilities with MPAS–O (vE3SM3.0.0)  – Part 2: Realistic experiments
abstract: River plumes can strongly influence coastal dynamics but are poorly resolved in global ocean models. Building on a companion study, we perform high-resolution simulations of the Mississippi–Atchafalaya (M–A) plume with the Model for Prediction Across Scales–Ocean (MPAS–O), a global model, and compare with a limited-domain Regional Ocean Modeling System configuration. MPAS–O qualitatively captures the M–A plume seasonality but fails to generate realistic eddies on the Texas–Louisiana shelf.

title: Evaluating the EPICC-Model for regional air quality simulation: a comparative study with CAMx and CMAQ
abstract: This study compares the model performance of the Emission and atmospheric Processes Integrated and Coupled Community Model with the two air quality models in China. The EPICC-Model excels in simulating summer ozone peaks, accurately captures pollution characteristics in highly polluted areas, and better reproduces persistent compound pollution processes. The study reveals common issues among the models and directions for improvement, providing a basis for optimizing global air quality models.

title: Physics vs. AI in weather prediction: evaluating GraphCast, AIFS, and FuXi against an observation-corrected WRF model for flash floods
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) weather models are now competing with traditional physics-based models for flood forecasting. We tested three of them and a physics-based model against observations from three flood events in Luxembourg. The AI models detected light rain and predicted temperatures better, but the physics-based model was more skilful at the heavy rainfall that actually causes floods. One AI model kept its skill on an event after its training period.

title: Improving snow simulations through improved representations of vegetation conditions: insights from high resolution simulations over California
abstract: Most hydrological models tend to underestimate snow over the mountainous southwestern US. This may result from uncertainties in precipitation forcing and/or inadequate representation of snow–vegetation interactions, particularly canopy interception and shading. Through model experiments, we demonstrate how downscaled meteorological forcing and improved vegetation representation can improve snow simulations over the southwestern US.

title: TRAILS – a novel framework for time-height-resolved attribution of long-range transported wildfire smoke
abstract: This research introduces a new method that combines model simulations with satellite observations to attribute the influence of wildfire smoke on an airmass. By dynamically determining the height of smoke plumes, we overcome a key limitation of earlier fixed reception-height approaches. This advancement is crucial for improving our understanding of how wildfire emissions influence cloud formation and the broader Earth's climate system.

title: Meso-NH-ISO v1.0: a water stable isotopologue scheme in the non-hydrostatic mesoscale atmospheric model Meso-NH – application to a 2D West African squall line
abstract: We implemented water stable isotopologues in the non-hydrostatic mesoscale atmospheric model Meso-NH. We validated this isotopic version (Meso-NH-ISO) with a simulation of a well-documented squall line in the Sahel region. In future works, simulations with Meso-NH-ISO will be done on real cases of cyclones or squall lines. The goal is to better interpret and quantify isotopic observations on the field in terms of atmospheric processes that drive development and intensity of those thunderstorms.
